newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Unions join Serbian demos against Milosevic.
newsitem.headline: Unions join Serbian demos against Milosevic.

text.p: An organised group of workers joined street protests against Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic on Wednesday for the first time since marches began 24 days ago, independent trade union leaders said.

Leaders of the association of independent trade unions said some 10,000 workers had been taking part in daily student and opposition rallies after the annulment of opposition local election victories by Milosevic's ruling socialists.
"We were also here before (as individuals) but for the first time today we are here in an organised way," association president Rade Radovanovic told Reuters.
Thousands of workers marched behind a trade union banner in a show of unity that Radovanovic earlier said would shake Milosevic and his deputies.
The West has supported demonstrations by up to 150,000 people a day in Belgrade but the mainly middle class protesters have failed to attract significant support from workers.
Independent unions claimed some of their 40,000 members in Belgrade had begun strike action citing the alleged election fraud among their grievances along with demands for pay.
"It is an old communist belief that when the workers come out against you, you are finished," Radovanovic said.

The Zajedno (Together) coalition of opposition parties on Tuesday lost its last legal appeal against the outcome of the November 17 elections, when the Yugoslav federal supreme court refused to intervene.
Political sources said Zajedno urgently needed to find new ways of maintaining the momentum of its campaign to drive Milosevic from power.
The United States and Europe have become increasingly vocal in their condemnation of Milosevic's tactics, threatening unspecified measures if he uses force to put down the marches.

In an interview with the CBS television network, U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher warned Milosevic that continuing his "repressive, undemocratic stance" would doom his dreams of ties to the West.
"He really is turning his back on opportunities to join the West, which I know is important to him," Christopher said.
He added the United States was considering reintroducing economic sanctions. The United Nations imposed sanctions on Yugoslavia for 3-1/2 years for its role in the war in Bosnia.
U.N. sanctions against Yugoslavia during the Bosnian war also targeted Montenegro, Serbia's partner in the Yugoslav federation, which is not involved in the election conflict.
The explicit talk of sanctions is the first hint that the West is serious about forcing Milosevic to back down and find a solution to the crisis.
The European Parliament also added its voice to cries of alarm, issuing a strongly-worded statement expressing deep concern about developments in Yugoslavia.

The parliamentarians' statement echoes a similar call from EU foreign ministers, who on December 6 postponed a decision to offer Serbia and Montenegro preferential trade terms already granted to other Balkan states.

Although the socialists used the courts to uphold the replacement by socialists of disqualified Zajedno councillors, an allied party of the socialists hinted a negotiated settlement was still within reach.
The Yugoslav United Left (JUL), which fought the elections in coalition with the Socialists, said a "common solution" was possible.
JUL president Ljubisa Ristic told the independent news agency Beta that "readiness for talks and agreements will mature slowly."
"In politics...there is a need to come to a solution so I believe that such a common solution will be reached however difficult, ugly, unpleasant and dramatic the situation may now seem."
